answer:
Take the axle’s motion as \(+x\) (to the right). For the usual forward-rolling rotation, the wheel rotates clockwise.

Angular period:
\[
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=\frac{2\pi}{8.0}=0.785\ \text{s}.
\]
The axle travels \(1.65\ \text{m}\) per revolution, so
\[
v_{\rm axle}=\frac{1.65}{T}
= \frac{1.65(8.0)}{2\pi}
\approx 2.10\ \text{m/s}.
\]

For pure rolling, the required axle speed would be
\[
v_{\rm pure}=R\omega=(0.30)(8.0)=2.40\ \text{m/s},
\]
and one revolution would carry the axle
\[
2\pi R=2\pi(0.30)\approx1.885\ \text{m}.
\]
But the observed distance is only \(1.65\ \text{m}\), so pure rolling does not fit.

At the bottom point,
\[
v_{\rm bottom}=v_{\rm axle}-R\omega
\approx 2.10-2.40=-0.30\ \text{m/s}.
\]
Thus the bottom/contact point has horizontal velocity
\[
\boxed{0.30\ \text{m/s opposite the axle’s motion, i.e. backward/left if the axle moves right}.}
\]

So the wheel is spinning too fast for its translational speed: the tire surface at the bottom slips backward relative to the ground. The magnitude of the slip velocity is about \(\boxed{0.30\ \text{m/s}}\). Pure rolling would require \(2.40\ \text{m/s}\) axle speed (or \(1.885\ \text{m}\) per revolution), not the observed \(2.10\ \text{m/s}\) (\(1.65\ \text{m}\) per revolution).
